# BandNine

> BandNine is an iPhone app for IELTS Speaking practice. Alex, an AI examiner, runs a timed Speaking test aloud: Part 1 questions, a Part 2 task card with 1 min to prepare and up to 2 min to speak, and a Part 3 discussion. The app then shows an estimated band for each of the four criteria (Fluency and coherence, Lexical resource, Grammatical range and accuracy, Pronunciation), with corrections that quote the candidate's own words. AI practice estimate. Not an official IELTS result.

- App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6825093223 (Android is in closed testing, not on Google Play yet)
- Website: https://bandnine.org/
- Questions and the examiner are in English; the app needs a microphone and an internet connection.
- BandNine is independent. IELTS is a registered trade mark of the British Council, IDP IELTS and Cambridge University Press & Assessment, and BandNine is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

## Questions about the app

- Is BandNine an official IELTS test? No. BandNine is a practice app. Every band it shows is an AI practice estimate, not an official IELTS result. Only the test you take at an IELTS centre gives you a band you can use.
- Who is Alex? Alex is the examiner in the app: an AI voice that runs the Speaking test in the same order as the real one. No person listens to your answers while you speak.
- How are the bands estimated? After the test, your transcript and the recording of your answers are scored against the four Speaking criteria: Fluency and coherence, Lexical resource, Grammatical range and accuracy, and Pronunciation. Each estimate comes with the words from your answers that support it. If there is not enough evidence for a criterion, the report says so instead of guessing.
- Can I practise one part at a time? Yes. You can take Part 1, Part 2 or Part 3 on its own, a full mock test of all three parts, or a two-minute quick drill of Part 1 questions on one topic.
- What does it cost? The app is free to download and every new account gets 17 credits, enough for one full mock test with its report. After that you get 2 free credits every Monday. More practice uses credit packs or BandNine Plus, weekly or monthly. The cost of each test is shown before you start.
- What happens if the connection drops during a test? If a test fails because of a fault on our side, the credits for it go back to your balance. If you leave early, you pay only for the parts you started, and the app shows that amount before you leave.
- Do I need an account? The app creates an anonymous account the first time you open it, so you can start without an email address. Link Apple or Google if you want to keep your history on a new phone.
- How do I delete my data? Open the You tab and tap Delete account. Your recordings, transcripts, band estimates and account are removed straight away. The delete-account page on this site explains how to ask by email instead.

## Guides to the IELTS Speaking test

- [IELTS fluency and coherence: keep your answers connected](https://bandnine.org/blog/ielts-fluency-and-coherence): Practise a steady pace, clear connections and brief repairs with recording drills that show why your answers pause or lose their thread. In short: Fluency depends on sustained speech and clear development, rather than a target speaking speed. Identify whether a pause comes from missing content or missing language before choosing a drill. Use connectors for a clear purpose and make pronoun references easy for the listener to follow. Keep repairs brief, then check whether the same habit works on an unfamiliar question.
- [IELTS pronunciation: what the examiner listens for](https://bandnine.org/blog/ielts-pronunciation): Practise word stress, sentence stress and pausing with spoken examples and a daily 10-minute drill focused on being understood. In short: Clear speech matters more than adopting a particular accent. Practise stress and pausing in complete answers, not only isolated words. Ask a listener which word they missed before choosing a drill. Check a new answer to see whether a practised feature transfers.
- [IELTS Speaking Band 7: what to listen for and practise](https://bandnine.org/blog/ielts-speaking-band-7): Understand Band 7 across the four Speaking criteria, identify a recurring difficulty and test your progress with a two-week recording routine. In short: Band 7 describes performance across a whole conversation, so a short example answer cannot demonstrate a band. The public descriptors give whole-band descriptions, without a separate description for Band 6.5. Choose one recurring difficulty and practise it across different questions before adding another target. Compare unfamiliar answers as well as repeated answers to check whether a skill transfers.
- [How the IELTS Speaking band descriptors work](https://bandnine.org/blog/ielts-speaking-band-descriptors): The four IELTS Speaking criteria in plain English, what separates Band 6 from Band 7 in each, and which one to practise first. In short: The four criteria carry equal weight, and your weakest one holds the overall band down more than your strongest lifts it. The test is marked as a whole, across all three parts, so a strong Part 1 is not enough and a weak start is not fatal. From Band 6 to Band 7, fluency means fewer restarts, vocabulary means natural collocation, and grammar means frequent error-free sentences. Pronunciation is judged on how easily you are understood and how you use stress and intonation, not on your accent.
- [IELTS Speaking Part 1: question types and how to answer](https://bandnine.org/blog/ielts-speaking-part-1-questions): Practise ten original Part 1 questions, choose a useful answer length and respond to changes in tense without memorising a script. In short: Give a direct answer and add a relevant detail when it helps explain your meaning. There is no fixed sentence count or duration for every Part 1 answer. Listen for changes in time before choosing your verbs. Use original practice questions to develop flexible answers rather than memorised speeches.
- [IELTS Speaking Part 2 topics: practise by category](https://bandnine.org/blog/ielts-speaking-part-2-topics): Twelve original Part 2 task cards grouped by topic, with advice on choosing relevant memories and adapting them to the exact prompt. In short: Use topic categories to find relevant memories without preparing complete speeches. The twelve original task cards are practice material, not predictions of test questions. Reuse a memory only when it answers the exact prompt and its explanation. Compare what the card asked you to explain with what you actually said.
- [IELTS Speaking Part 2: a cue card technique for the full two minutes](https://bandnine.org/blog/ielts-speaking-part-2-cue-card-technique): How to use the minute of preparation, what to write on the paper, a shape for the talk, and what to do when the story runs out before two minutes. In short: Read the top line of the card twice, choose the first real example that comes to mind, and stay with it. Write single words, one line per point on the card, plus one line for the final point, which asks you to explain. Name it, set the scene, tell what happened with one detail, bring in the other person, then explain and come up to the present. When the story runs out, add a reason, an example, a contrast, a then-and-now, or a feeling; each gives you thirty more seconds.
- [IELTS Speaking Part 3: discuss unfamiliar ideas](https://bandnine.org/blog/ielts-speaking-part-3-discussion): Learn to develop Part 3 answers with reasons, comparisons and careful speculation, using original practice questions and short candidate examples. In short: Part 3 moves beyond personal experience to broader discussion linked to Part 2. Identify whether the question asks for a cause, comparison, proposal or possibility. Develop one relevant point before adding another. Use conditionals and cautious language when discussing imagined situations. Practise follow-up questions to develop ideas without memorising complete answers.
- [IELTS Speaking preparation: a four-week study plan](https://bandnine.org/blog/ielts-speaking-study-plan): Follow a four-week Speaking plan with daily 20-minute sessions, one criterion per week and mock tests that check progress on new questions. In short: Start with an uninterrupted mock test and record specific difficulties. Give each week one main criterion while continuing to answer complete questions. Use daily 20-minute sessions for a drill, fresh speaking and review. Compare different questions to check whether practice carries into unfamiliar answers. Keep the final three days focused on familiar routines.
- [The IELTS Speaking test, part by part](https://bandnine.org/blog/ielts-speaking-test-format): Understand the three parts, their timing, the task card and the discussion, with practical advice for your Speaking appointment. In short: The Speaking test lasts 11–14 minutes and has the same format for Academic and General Training. Part 2 includes 1 minute to prepare, a long turn and brief rounding-off questions. The examiner manages the time and assesses your English across the whole test. Practise changing your answer length as the test moves between parts.
